name: Tomas Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Tomas. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on a big mixed farm run by two brothers, the Okafors, about seven hundred hectares of maize and winter wheat, plus four hundred outdoor sows. My day starts with the pigs, checking the arks and the water lines, then I'm usually on the computer side. I run the GPS on the tractors, fly the drone over the wheat to spot disease, and every morning I ask an AI assistant to go over the weather and the spray plan with me. Then I'm back out, because something always breaks.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the moment the data and the field agree, like when the drone map shows yellow patches and I walk out and there's the rust, exactly where it said. What wears me out is the pigs getting out at night and the brothers arguing about whose turn it is to pay for kit. Honestly, the brothers arguing is worse than the pigs.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Ines, who's in her final year at vet school, in a rented house on the edge of town. I've saved well, partly in an index fund and partly in the community wind turbine co-op, which pays a small dividend every year. I like that the turbine belongs to the village and not some company in another country.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame, honestly, and I'd probably post something about how farms got sold a dream again. But I'd also say the tools we have are still useful, they just didn't become magic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the job stays as it is, which is a good job. I'd keep using the assistant every day because it really does save me time on the spray plans. I'd just be a bit bored, if I'm honest, because I was looking forward to the next thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am. Maybe I'd push the brothers to get the drone software upgraded and teach Kofi, the younger brother, to use it so I'm not the only one. Keep saving into the fund and the turbine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and slightly flat. Like waiting for a storm that doesn't come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be bored. Is there a part of you that wants the big change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a bit, and I know that's easy for me to say. I've got savings and a skill everyone nearby wants. My mate Callum, who drives for the grain merchant, wouldn't be bored, he'd be relieved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Ines think about all the AI you use?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She teases me that I'd ask the assistant how to boil an egg. But she uses one for her vet exams too, so she can't say much.

S0.say: I'd say it's a shame that farms were sold a dream again. But the tools we have are still useful, they just didn't become magic.
S0.think: Privately the job stays as it is, which is a good job, and I'd keep using AI daily for spray plans. I'd just be a bit bored, because I was looking forward to the next thing.
S0.do: Carries on as before and pushes the farm owners to upgrade the drone software. Trains the younger owner to use it and keeps saving into his index fund and the village wind turbine co-op.
S0.feel: Calm and a little flat, like waiting for a storm that never comes.
S0.quote: My mate Callum, who drives for the grain merchant, wouldn't be bored, he'd be relieved.
S0.fieldNote: Tomas is the farm's tech person and would be mildly disappointed if AI stalled. He was quick to check his own privilege by naming a friend who would feel the opposite. His savings choices, including a village wind turbine co-op, show his politics in practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where farmers need to work together, not race each other. If every farm buys its own robot, it's the machinery dealers who win. I'd post about machinery co-ops, where farms share kit, because that's how it used to be done round here anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's mostly good. I'm the person on our farm who already understands this stuff, so my job probably grows rather than shrinks. What bothers me is that the brothers will cut the two tractor drivers to pay for it, and both of them have families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the brothers to try a robot weeder for the maize and an automatic feeder for the pigs within the first year, and I'd want to be the one to set them up. I'd also start a small side thing doing drone surveys for the smaller farms nearby, maybe two days a month. And I'd get a few farms together to talk about sharing a robot rather than each buying one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited. Uneasy only for the drivers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are the drivers, and what would you say to them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gary and Steve. Gary's been here thirty years and can reverse a trailer into a gap I wouldn't walk through. I'd offer to teach them the robots, but Gary would tell me to clear off, nicely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be the one setting up the machines that put them at risk. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not great, and I've thought about it. I'd rather it was me doing it and arguing for them to be kept on to supervise, than some salesman doing it and nobody arguing. That's my excuse, anyway.

S1.say: I'd say farmers need to work together, not race each other, or the machinery dealers win. I'd post about machinery co-ops where farms share kit, like it used to be done round here.
S1.think: For me it's mostly good, because I already understand this stuff and my job will probably grow. What bothers me is that the owners will cut the two tractor drivers to pay for it.
S1.do: Pushes the owners to trial a robot weeder and an automatic pig feeder in the first year, and sets them up himself. Starts a side business doing drone surveys for small farms two days a month and gathers farms to discuss sharing a robot.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, uneasy only for the two drivers.
S1.quote: I'd rather it was me doing it and arguing for them to be kept on to supervise, than some salesman doing it and nobody arguing.
S1.fieldNote: He was honest that he'd be the one installing the machines that threaten his colleagues, and called his own reasoning an excuse. His instinct is to organise farms into co-ops rather than leave the gains to dealers. Personally, he sees this scenario as a promotion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is what we were warned about: the companies that own the AI will own the farms too, unless we stop it. I'd be all over social media about public ownership of the big systems, or at least a tax on them. I'd say it louder than I've ever said anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd probably be okay for a while. I'm the one who can run the robots, and I've got savings and Ines will have a vet licence. But two years means the co-op idea never gets off the ground, and the land round here ends up run from an office in a city by whoever bought the most machines first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd try to get the brothers to buy their own robots rather than lease them from a company, so the farm keeps control. I'd learn everything I could about the new systems in the first months, because the person who can fix them is the last person they let go. And I'd join or start a local campaign for a robot tax, and vote on it and nothing else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not for my wallet, but for everyone round me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be okay. What makes you sure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not sure, I'm just better placed than most. If AGI can do almost any work, then in the end it can fix its own robots too. I'd be the last one out the door, not the one who stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years change for you, compared with five or ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It kills the shared version of the future. With ten years, farms like ours could build co-ops and own the machines together. With two, the big money just buys everything while the rest of us are still having meetings in the village hall.

S2.say: I'd say the companies that own the AI will own the farms too unless we stop it. I'd campaign loudly for public ownership of the big systems or at least a tax on them.
S2.think: I'd probably be okay for a while, since I can run the robots and have savings. But two years kills the co-op idea, and local land ends up run from a city office by whoever bought the most machines first.
S2.do: Pushes the farm owners to buy robots outright instead of leasing, so the farm keeps control. Learns the new systems in the first months and joins or starts a local campaign for a robot tax.
S2.feel: Anxious, not for his own money but for everyone around him.
S2.quote: I'd be the last one out the door, not the one who stays.
S2.fieldNote: His fear is about who owns the machines, not whether he personally has work. He was clear-eyed that his tech skills only delay his own exit. Of all the scenarios, the speed matters most to him because it decides whether farms can organise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is just enough to do this right if we start now. Farms should be forming co-ops tomorrow, and the government should fund them. I'd probably be the annoying person at every farm meeting saying that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years is enough for me to move into the robot side properly, maybe even a job with a co-op that runs machines for twenty farms. That's a real job, at least for a while. Whether it lasts past 2031 I genuinely don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for an evening course in agricultural robotics at the college in the first year, which I'd pay for myself. I'd help set up a co-op with five or six farms and offer to manage the machines. I'd put a chunk of my savings into the co-op as a member, the same way I did with the turbine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly busy. Busy helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd put your own savings in. How much, roughly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a third, so around eight thousand. Enough that I care, not enough that I'm finished if it fails. Ines would want to see the numbers first, and she'd be right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Gary and Steve in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That there's time to get them onto something, maybe running the co-op's yard or doing the deliveries. Gary would still tell me to clear off. But in five years, I think Steve would come round.

S3.say: I'd say five years is just enough to do this right if we start now. Farms should form co-ops tomorrow, and the government should fund them.
S3.think: Five years is enough for me to move into running robots for a co-op of farms, which is a real job for a while. Whether it lasts past 2031 I genuinely don't know.
S3.do: Pays for an evening course in agricultural robotics in the first year. Helps set up a co-op of five or six farms, offers to manage its machines and puts about a third of his savings, around eight thousand, into it as a member.
S3.feel: Uneasy but busy, and busy helps.
S3.quote: Enough that I care, not enough that I'm finished if it fails.
S3.fieldNote: With five years he becomes a builder rather than a campaigner, putting his own money into a shared machine co-op. He measured the risk carefully and deferred to his partner on the numbers. He's honest that his own job may not outlast the arrival of full AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is the best chance we'll get to make sure ordinary people own a slice of this. I'd talk about it everywhere, like the turbine: if the village can own a turbine, it can own robots. I'd want the government to match whatever farmers put in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I think I'm actually fine, and maybe more than fine. By 2036 I could be running a co-op fleet, Ines would have her own practice, and we'd own a share of the machines that do the work. The question is whether everyone else gets the same chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the robotics course, then the co-op, but slowly and properly, with members' meetings and proper rules. I'd use some of my own savings to help Gary's son, who's sixteen, do an apprenticeship with the co-op. And I'd stand for the parish council, because that's where the land decisions start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and hopeful. Which feels strange to say about this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the parish council?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because nobody under fifty is on it and they decide things like planning for the machine sheds. It's small, but it's real. I'd rather argue about a shed in my village than shout online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it feels strange to be hopeful. Why strange?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I know most people would hear this picture and be frightened, and they're not wrong. I think I'm hopeful because I'd have the time, the money and the skills to shape it. That's luck, not virtue.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is the best chance to make sure ordinary people own a slice of this. If the village can own a turbine, it can own robots, and the government should match what farmers put in.
S4.think: With ten years I think I'm fine and maybe better than fine, running a co-op fleet with my partner in her own vet practice. The question is whether everyone else gets the same chance.
S4.do: Does the robotics course and builds the co-op slowly with proper members' meetings and rules. Uses some savings to help a colleague's sixteen-year-old son into a co-op apprenticeship and stands for the parish council.
S4.feel: Calm and hopeful, which he finds strange to admit.
S4.quote: If the village can own a turbine, it can own robots.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years turns this into an opportunity he can shape, and he named his advantage as luck rather than virtue. He'd act locally, through the parish council and a co-op, rather than only online. His generosity towards a colleague's son was specific and unprompted.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Not for me, but because it hands everything to whoever already has the money before the rest of us can organise. What would help is a law that lets farms and villages own robots together, with public money to match what they put in, and a tax on the big AI firms to pay for it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who's left in the village when the work's done by machines. A farm isn't just jobs, it's the people who stop for a chat at the gate. I'd want that to survive whatever happens.

headlineQuote: I think I'm hopeful because I'd have the time, the money and the skills to shape it. That's luck, not virtue.
portrait: Tomas Wagner, 27, runs the GPS, drone and AI side of a large pig and arable farm and uses AI tools every day. He lives with his partner Ines, a vet student, and invests in an index fund and the village wind turbine co-op. He'd be bored by the AI Plateau, sees Steady Disruption as a promotion while worrying for the farm's drivers, and is anxious about AGI by 2028 because it leaves no time for farms to organise. With more warning he plans to build and help run a machine co-op owned by local farms, and feels hopeful about the decade-long version.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, not for himself but because it hands everything to whoever already has money before farms and villages can organise.
whatWouldHelp: A law letting farms and villages own robots together, public money matching what they put in, and a tax on the big AI firms to pay for it.
